newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai baht dives to record low, intervention.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai baht dives to record low, intervention.

text.p: Thailand's beleaguered baht plunged to a record low in the local market on Wednesday, forcing central bank intervention to arrest the currency's worst slide since it went into a managed float on July 2.

Dealers said the baht's dive in the thinly traded onshore market was mainly due to a scramble for dollars by local importers seeking the U.S. unit to pay bills and by corporates needing the greenback to repay foreign loans.
Some dealers reported baht/dollar deals done at a level as low as 32.60 to the dollar before the Bank of Thailand's defence of the currency through dollar sales.
"We noticed the central bank intervened to stop the baht's fall at around the 32.50/32.60 (bid/ask) to the dollar level," a senior dealer with a local bank told Reuters.
Others said the central bank did not have to sell many dollars to curb the baht's fall.
This was because pressure on the currency was mainly from local players trading in relatively small amounts and the currency's movement was exaggerated in a thin market.
After the intervention by around 0925 GMT, the baht steadied and was quoted at around 32.21/32.41 against the dollar in the domestic market and stronger at 31.45/31.55 in the offshore market.
Thai central bank officials were not available for comment on the reported intervention.
Thailand's stock market plummeted more than four percent, in part due to worries about the baht, brokers said. It closed down 28.50 points to 631.28.
The baht's tumble comes as Thailand goes through its worst economic slump in more than a decade and its financial sector faces numerous troubles.
The baht was released into a managed float by Thailand after being pegged for 13 years to a trade-weighted basket of currencies dominated by the dollar.
Since the flotation, the baht has undergone a de facto devaluation of about 20 percent.
Dealers and a senior Thai central bank official also attributed poor baht sentiment to weak first-half earnings results reported by local banks and finance firms this week.
"I think this is mainly a result of the bank's results we saw yesterday and that knocked the fragile confidence that had crept back in," said one Singapore based analyst.
"If you look at the results of the banks there are some horror stories in terms of earnings per share."

With the corporate market still squeezed there was still a cash-flow problem. That, on top of the bad balance sheet issue made worse by the devaluation of offshore liabilities, had led to a scramble for dollars in short supply, he said.

Thanasak Chantarovat, deputy director of the central bank's banking department, said the baht could also have been hurt by negative expectations about data on the level of non-performing loans of financial institutions due to be released soon.
The data is due to be announced through the stock exchange on Thursday, a local banker said.

Financial markets have been waiting nervously to gauge the level of non-performing loans by banks and finance firms, which are overexposed with billions of dollars in sour loans to the depressed and cash-strapped property sector.
Some dealers said they saw an appropriate level for the baht at between 30.50-31.50 to the dollar in the near term, given current concerns over the Thai economy and problems in the financial sector.
